passage: Pablo pressed his forehead against the cold window of the hospital corridor in Lima. His grandfather lay in a room down the hall with tubes and a beeping machine. Pablo's stomach felt tight all day. His cousin Jamal was coloring on a napkin, but Pablo could not draw. Finally he walked up to the nurse at the desk and asked, "Is my grandfather going to die?" The nurse crouched down and said the doctors were working hard, that they did not know yet, and that he could sit with his grandfather for a few minutes. Pablo nodded. It was scary, but it was better than guessing.

qa.q: Which city is the hospital in?
What was Pablo feeling as he stood at the window, and what shows it?
qa.a: He was afraid; his stomach felt tight all day and he could not draw like Jamal.

qa.q: What did Pablo do that helped him, and why did it work?
qa.a: He asked the nurse an honest question directly. Getting a truthful answer, even an uncertain one, was easier for him than imagining the worst.

qa.q: How might the nurse have seen Pablo's question?
qa.a: The nurse may have seen a frightened child who deserved a truthful, gentle answer rather than a brush-off, and who could cope better once he knew where things stood.

grounding: A child afraid his grandfather may die asks an adult honest questions and sits with him; not knowing is scarier.

passage: When Dadaji went into hospital with his heart, everyone at home spoke in low voices and stopped talking when I came in. My name is Pranav, and that silence frightened me more than anything. I lay awake thinking, what if he dies and nobody tells me? On the third day I asked Ramesh Chacha straight out, 'Is Dadaji going to die?' He didn't laugh or change the subject. He said, 'His heart is weak, and the doctors are working hard. We don't know yet. I'll tell you when we know more.' It was scary, but less scary than the silence. That evening Chacha took me to the hospital. I held Dadaji's hand and showed him my drawing of our mango tree. He squeezed my fingers.

qa.a: A drawing of their mango tree.

qa.q: Why did the silence at home frighten Pranav?
qa.a: Pranav felt afraid and shut out, lying awake worried that Dadaji might die without anyone saying so.
Asking Ramesh Chacha an honest question, getting a truthful answer, then visiting Dadaji to hold his hand and share a drawing.

qa.q: What might Dadaji have felt when Pranav held his hand?
qa.a: Comforted and loved; he squeezed Pranav's fingers.

grounding: A child afraid a grandfather may die asks an adult an honest question, gets a truthful answer, and sits with him.

passage:
Class 3 teacher's note, by Nazia Siddiqui.
Vishal was quiet all morning and drew the same picture three times: a bed with a small figure in it. At break I sat with him. 'My Nanaji is in hospital,' he whispered. 'Nobody tells me anything. Is he going to die?' His lip was trembling. I told him I did not know, that it was a good question, and that the people who could answer it were his parents. With his permission I phoned his mother at lunch. She came at home time and knelt beside him. 'Nanaji is very ill, and the doctors are helping him. You can visit on Sunday and take your drawing.' Vishal held her hand tightly and asked two more questions. She answered both.

qa.q: What did Vishal draw three times?
qa.a: A bed with a small figure in it.

qa.q: What did Vishal's trembling lip show?
qa.a: He was frightened that Nanaji might die and upset that nobody was telling him anything.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that helped?
qa.a: Sat with Vishal, admitted not knowing, and phoned his mother that day so she could give him simple, honest answers.

qa.q: How might his mother have felt learning Vishal was so worried?
qa.a: Probably sorry she hadn't explained sooner and eager to comfort him, since she came, knelt and answered his questions.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a boy frightened about his grandfather's illness, and adults giving him honest answers the same day.
